dossier.public_summary: The dip changes dramatically from one sector and transit to the next and one transit is almost absent - from ~8000 ppm to ~1500 ppm over 118% - which real planets do not do. Even though the shape looks flat and no nearby eclipsing stars could cause it, the depth is not stable, so this is best explained as a spot or noise fluctuation rather than a planet on the M-dwarf.

reasons.why: 5 transits are inconsistent, driven by one outlier at 257 ppm vs ~4900 ppm on others (share_of_top_3 0.95, chi2 44.49 dof 4). A planet dip should repeat; this is a few-bad-transit / noise signature, not steady planetary transits.

Depth changes by ~118% between sectors: 1488 +/-763 ppm (24), 7761 +/-942 ppm (50), 8126 +/-985 ppm (77), 5121 +/-863 ppm (78), chi2 39.82 dof 3. Sector depth tool says changes_within_a_source with p_constant 1.1590543496822076e-08, so depth does not simply vary between pipelines but varies within TESS-SPOC, opposite of a consistent planet.

Odd-even depth difference is 5602 ppm even 3809 ppm (+1793 ppm, ratio 1.5) at 1.987 sigma overall; planet case not confirmed and depth instability remains, with sector_oe_max_sigma 1.909 inconsistent with flat bottoms.

Difference imaging has no sector with clear detection and centroid_all not_run, so on-target is not established; neighbours plausible_within_1px 0 at distance 95.11 can be ruled out as blend but cannot prove a planet on target without a stable dip.

Independent scorer rates this as planet-like as few known planets, consistent with depth variability and outlier transit outweighing a flat shape (shape v_sigma -2.561) and small size (rp_rearth 3.196) that alone are insufficient without stable depth. Duration ratio 1.49 (stellar_radius TIC 0.4165) also shows high impact parameter/bump rather than a secure fit.
